description: We are a parent-and-teen homeschooling family team passionate about space exploration, STEAM learning, and creative problem-solving. We bring a blend of software development, web prototyping, and educational project design, paired with curiosity, fresh perspectives, and strong self-driven learning.
summary: Three cat astronauts. Seven sols. One Mars outpost. A 10-minute browser game where kids 7–12 keep a base alive by making real trade-offs with NASA data. Bilingual EN/zh-TW, with hands-on mini-games.
details:
Meowstronauts: Mars Outpost

What it does

Meowstronauts: Mars Outpost is a free, bilingual browser game for children ages 7–12, built for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Three cat astronauts crash-land beside a fictional Mars outpost and must keep it — and themselves — alive for seven sols, until a supply ship arrives. A run takes about ten minutes, and a skippable six-scene opening sets up the crash before the first decision.

Each sol, the player reads the captain's log with that day's weather, then faces one event card and chooses one action from it — usually one of three. Every action helps one system and costs another: sweeping dust off the solar panels restores power but tires the crew; thickening the shelter wall spends 20 power and adds 25 radiation shielding. Power, life support, shielding, food and health drift down every sol, and a system that reaches zero starts hurting the crew. At the end, the mission report gives a star rating, the seven-sol resource curve, and the cats' verdict on your command. Three difficulty levels — Cadet, Officer and Ace — change the starting reserves, so the same deck can play gently or tightly.

Eleven mini-games rehearse the hard parts: sweeping solar panels, patching a hull breach, a shelter drill, a low-gravity hop, a Mars weather landing, a water-and-fuel factory, space-food flip, tomato harvest, dust-devil dodge and a knowledge-card match. Some open inside an event and some from the captain's log; none is a dead end — the story always continues.

How it works

Real NASA archives drive the situation, not just the decoration. The fixed Sol 4 flare alert is the 14 May 2025 X2.7 flare from NASA's DONKI archive, and the seven sols run across the 15–22 May 2025 cold week recorded by Curiosity's REMS station, with daily highs between −33 °C and −26 °C. Mars surface photographs from the NASA Image Library appear in the rest-day album, each with its NASA ID and credit. The data panel charts the DONKI flare sequence and the REMS temperature curve, labelled "snapshot, not live". Snapshots are fetched by a local Node script before the event and committed as JSON, so no NASA feed has to be up for the mission to run. An optional "latest weather" section in the data panel can query NASA's public REMS feed on request; if it fails, it shows an archived copy clearly marked as such, and it never changes the mission.

Terms in the text are tappable: a definition opens in a side panel with its NASA source and can be saved to a backpack. Twenty knowledge cards are collectable in all. Nothing is forced — the game is fully playable without opening a single card.

The game is a static React build served by Cloudflare Workers at mars.flymymind.com, deployed from GitHub by Workers Builds on every push that passes tests and build. There are no accounts and no uploads; language choice and the backpack live in localStorage only. No AI runs at runtime.

Why it works

- The cost is on the button. Every choice shows its resource chips before the player commits, so the trade-off is felt in the interface, not explained in a lecture.

- Failure is gentle. A drained system hurts the crew, but the game pauses the mission and offers a debrief instead of a scolding.

- Reading is optional. Knowledge cards never block the next sol, so a child who only wants the game can ignore all twenty.

- One ten-minute run fits a class period or a car ride, and there is nothing to install, sign up for, or pay.

- The same build works on a phone in landscape, a tablet or a classroom projector: layouts are verified from 568×320 to 1440×900, with 44 px minimum touch targets and reduced-motion support.

- English and Traditional Chinese are complete, with English as the default.

Why it matters

Mission teams divide scarce electricity among crew systems, communications and research, and balance radiation risk against mission goals. Most youth-facing space content either simplifies those trade-offs away or assumes too much technical knowledge. Here the rules carry the lesson: every choice has a visible cost, every resource is connected, and the player learns a real deep-space constraint by feeling it. The NASA data gives that feeling a factual anchor — the flare and the cold week really happened — and the "snapshot, not live" label teaches the difference between an archive, a forecast and a live feed.

Tools, languages and hardware

- Game: React 19 + TypeScript 5.9, built with Vite 8; hand-written CSS, no UI framework or icon library

- Hosting: Cloudflare Workers static assets via Wrangler, custom domain mars.flymymind.com, continuous deployment from GitHub by Workers Builds

- NASA data: DONKI (13–17 May 2025), Curiosity REMS (8–22 May 2025) and NASA Image Library photographs, fetched by a local Node script and committed as JSON; no API key ships to the browser

- Content: 13 event cards (including a scripted Sol 1 tutorial), 20 knowledge cards, a six-scene opening and ten mini-games, fully bilingual

- Quality: 254 Vitest unit and integration tests across 37 files, plus 13 Playwright end-to-end tests across 7 spec files (full seven-sol run, both languages, responsive layouts, demo-video route); GitHub Actions runs lint, tests and build on every push to main and every pull request

- Supporting tools: Node.js for the snapshot fetcher; Python (Pillow, rembg) and FFmpeg for brand art and the 30-second demo video

- License: Apache-2.0

- Hardware: none beyond a browser — any modern phone, tablet or laptop, with no sensor, controller or install

Source code
